Q: "OSS support for Spring Boot 3.5.x ended on 2026-06-30" message doesn't go away after upgrading to 4.1.0 A:

BOOT_VERSION_VALIDATION_CODE is a VS Code/Spring Boot Tools diagnostic, not a Gradle build error or a Spring Boot runtime message. In the build.gradle shown, both the Boot plugin and the Boot BOM are already on 4.1.0:

id "org.springframework.boot" version "4.1.0"
mavenBom 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:4.1.0'

So the remaining OSS support for Spring Boot 3.5.x ended on 2026-06-30 marker is stale editor metadata. Refresh the VS Code Java/Spring project state:

Ctrl+Shift+P
Java: Reload Projects
Java: Clean Java Language Server Workspace
Reload and delete

Then reopen the workspace if VS Code does not reload it automatically.

Spring Tools has a Spring Boot version validation feature that checks versions in build files. When its cached view of the Gradle project is stale, the old 3.5.x diagnostic can remain attached to the plugins block even though the file now says 4.1.0.

Changing gradle.properties will not affect this warning. The diagnostic text is specifically about the Spring Boot version, not Gradle 9.3.1.

Q: Why do these two sets of Linq code not work the same? A:

The two versions aren't doing the same thing. In the first one, continue skips any property that's in nullableNames, so it processes everything else. In the second one, Where(p => nullableNames.Contains(p.Name)) keeps only those properties. If you want the same behavior, use:

foreach (var prop in properties.Where(p => !nullableNames.Contains(p.Name)))

For example, if nullableNames = ["Name"], the first version processes Age, Email, etc., while the second version processes only Name. The missing ! is the difference.

Q: In Perl array, Range "-1" used to be the last element A:

Use @A[ 3 .. $#A ]

@A[ EXPR1 .. EXPR2 ] isn't some special array slicing notation.

EXPR1 .. EXPR2 is the range operator. It will produce an ascending sequence of integers from EXPR1 to EXPR2 (inclusive).[1] This is impossible when EXPR1 is larger than EXPR2 as is the case in your code. It generates zero integers in that case.

So yes, providing -1 as an index would refer to the last element of the array, but you don't generate the value -1.

You can use $#A or @A-1 to obtain the last index of an array.

  1. It has another mode where it can generate strings, but that's not relevant here.

Q: C++ compile error: 'Player' does not name a type when using one class inside another A:

Player needs to be visible when screenWindow.h is compiled. If screenWindow stores a Player object (not a pointer/reference), you need to #include "Character.h" in screenWindow.h. If you only need to refer to the player, storing a Player* or Player& is usually a better design and avoids circular include issues.

Q: Remove multiple occurrences of similar lines except the last A:

All you need is:

awk '/^2026-/{s=$0 ORS; next} {print s $0; s=""}' file

The above will work using any awk in a single pass of the input and only storing 1 date-line in memory at a time.

That is accommodating the OPs comment:

In my scenario, if the last line was a timestamp, then I would not be interested in it.

but if they did want to print a date-line if it appeared at the end of the input, it'd be a trivial tweak to add an END statment:

awk '/^2026-/{s=$0 ORS; next} {print s $0; s=""} END{printf "%s", s}' file

Here it is running on the OPs provided sample input:

$ awk '/^2026-/{s=$0 ORS; next} {print s $0; s=""}' file
important information 1
important information 2
2026-07-10T11:15:09.647148-04:00     <-- keep
important information 3
important information 4
important information 5
2026-07-10T11:15:12.662378-04:00     <-- keep
important information 6
important information 7
2026-07-10T11:15:18.232970-04:00     <-- keep
important information 8
2026-07-10T11:30:22.788192-04:00     <-- keep
important information 9
important information 10
important information 11

The problem with the OPs tac file.txt | awk '/2026-/ {if (f) next; f=1}1' | tac command was they never resent their f flag to zero. Personally I'd use a counter to keep track of the number of date-lines in the current block instead of just a flag for that sort of approach (not handling the date-line at end of input case as this approach isn't necessary anyway):

$ tac file | awk '{c=(/^2026-/ ? c+1 : 0)} c<2' | tac
important information 1
important information 2
2026-07-10T11:15:09.647148-04:00     <-- keep
important information 3
important information 4
important information 5
2026-07-10T11:15:12.662378-04:00     <-- keep
important information 6
important information 7
2026-07-10T11:15:18.232970-04:00     <-- keep
important information 8
2026-07-10T11:30:22.788192-04:00     <-- keep
important information 9
important information 10
important information 11

but as shown above we don't need multiple commands and pipelines to solve this problem.

Q: SQL Syntax - Matching Tables/Columns A:

You can use unnest(array(...)) and compare each pattern with column name

select table_name, column_name ,elem
from information_schema.columns t 
join lateral (
    SELECT elem FROM unnest(array['%price%','%parent%','%product%']) AS elem 
)p on column_name ILike elem
;

If columns patterns is a query parameter

select table_name, column_name ,elem
from information_schema.columns t 
join lateral (
    SELECT elem FROM unnest(STRING_TO_ARRAY('%price%,%parent%,%product%',',')) AS elem 
)p on column_name ILike elem
;

However, if the column name matches several templates, you will get several rows per column.

Aggregate by table_name, column_name

select table_name, column_name ,string_agg(elem,',') pattern
from information_schema.columns t 
join lateral (
    SELECT elem FROM unnest(STRING_TO_ARRAY('%price%,%parent%,%product%,%node%',',')) AS elem 
)p on column_name ILike elem
group by table_name,column_name
;
